h1: The 8 Best Docking Stations for MacBook Air of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: MacBook Air Docking Stations: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 docking stations for MacBook Air, from a certified Plugable Thunderbolt 4 dock to DisplayLink hubs, scored on displays.
summary: The Plugable Thunderbolt 4 Dock (TBT-UDM) is the best choice for a MacBook Air owner who wants one rock-solid monitor, 100W charging and no drivers. If you need two screens, the TobenONE 18-in-2 uses DisplayLink to get past the Air's single-display limit. The Anker DL6350 goes to three displays. On a budget, the PULWTOP gives dual 4K for little, and the UGREEN Revodok Pro 210 is the pocket-size option for one extra screen.
intro: The MacBook Air has one hard limit that decides which dock you should buy. Out of the box, it drives a single external display natively on most chips. Every dock that advertises dual monitors on an Air is either quietly relying on DisplayLink software or is simply wrong for your machine.

We reviewed eight docks and hubs across that split: one certified Thunderbolt dock for a clean single or 6K display, and seven USB-C hubs, most using DisplayLink to add screens. Rankings are based on spec sheets and owner-reported behavior, with display method, charging power and driver requirements weighed ahead of raw port count.

products.name: Plugable Thunderbolt 4 Dock for M4/M5 MacBook Air & Pro (TBT-UDM)
products.verdict: Certified Thunderbolt 4, 100W charging and a driverless setup.
products.description:
Plugable's TBT-UDM is a certified Thunderbolt 4 dock at 40Gbps with 100W charging, dual 4K HDMI or one 6K display, six USB ports, an SD slot and Ethernet. It uses the full Thunderbolt connection, not a slower USB-C Alt Mode link, and needs no drivers.

It wins because a certified controller makes the connection stable, and it is the only dock here built for the newer Thunderbolt Airs. The DisplayLink hubs below can add screens but compress video, and the TobenONE adds a driver.

Best for Air owners who want a single high-quality monitor and a fast dock. Caveat: older Airs may limit dual monitors natively.
cons: Dual display depends on the chip
products.idealFor: Newer Airs with one high-quality monitor.
products.skipIf: Your Air has no Thunderbolt port.

products.name: TobenONE 18-in-2 Docking Station Dual Monitor for MacBook Pro/Air
products.verdict: DisplayLink dual 4K at 60Hz with a 150W power adapter and 2.5G Ethernet.
products.description:
The TobenONE 18-in-2 uses DisplayLink to push a second 4K at 60Hz signal past the Air's native limit, through HDMI and USB-C. It includes a 150W power adapter, seven USB ports, 10Gbps USB-C, 2.5G Ethernet and an SD 4.0 reader.

It ranks second because it solves the Air's real problem: a second monitor. The 17-in-2 sibling is close but older, and the PULWTOP gives the same dual 4K for less with fewer ports.

Best for an Air owner who needs two screens at a desk. Caveat: DisplayLink needs a driver and compresses video slightly.
products.idealFor: Air owners who need two external screens.

products.name: Anker Docking Station DL6350, 10-Port Triple Display with DisplayLink
products.verdict: Three displays through DisplayLink with dual HDMI and DisplayPort.
products.description:
Anker's DL6350 goes to three displays through DisplayLink, using dual HDMI plus DisplayPort across 10 ports. It works with Windows and MacBook Air and Pro, and DisplayLink's driver is mature.

It places third because three screens is a niche need, and the TobenONE gives two screens with more ports and power for less. If you actually want three monitors, nothing else here does it.

Best for a trading or monitoring desk with three displays on an Air. Caveat: the driver and compression apply to all three.
cons: Higher price for a niche need
products.idealFor: Three-monitor desks on a MacBook Air.

products.name: WAVLINK USB C Docking Station Dual Monitor, Dual 5K/4K@60Hz
products.verdict: Dual displays up to 5K, with HDMI and DisplayPort and 130W charging.
products.description:
The WAVLINK 13-in-1 supports two displays up to 5K through DisplayLink, with two HDMI and two DisplayPort outputs, 130W Power Delivery, five USB ports and audio. It covers M1 to M4 Macs as well as Windows.

It ranks fourth because a 5K ceiling matters to few owners, and the TobenONE offers 2.5G Ethernet and a bigger adapter. The mixed outputs mean you can pair different monitors without adapters.

Best for a mixed HDMI and DisplayPort monitor pair. Caveat: it needs the DisplayLink driver.

products.name: TobenONE 17-IN-2 MacBook Docking Station Dual 4K Monitor
products.verdict: Dual 4K, a 150W charger and compatibility from M1 through M5.
products.description:
The TobenONE 17-in-2 offers dual 4K through DisplayLink, a 150W charger included, seven USB ports up to 10Gbps and 2.5G Ethernet. The listing states compatibility with M1 through M5 chips.

It ranks fifth because the 18-in-2 sits above it in the same line with a USB-C display output. Compared with the PULWTOP below, it adds a bigger charger and faster Ethernet.

Best for owners of an older Air who want a bundled charger. Caveat: still a DisplayLink design.
products.idealFor: Older and newer Airs sharing one desk.
products.skipIf: You want a native Thunderbolt link.

products.name: PULWTOP MacBook Pro Docking Station Dual Monitor 4K@60Hz
products.verdict: Dual HDMI at 4K and 60Hz for under $100.
products.description:
The PULWTOP gives you dual HDMI at 4K and 60Hz, 10Gbps USB-A and USB-C data, an SD and TF slot, a USB 2.0 port, Ethernet and PD charging passthrough. It uses DisplayLink for the second screen.

It ranks sixth because the bigger TobenONE models add chargers and faster Ethernet. It is the cheapest way to get two screens on an Air.

Best for a budget dual monitor desk. Caveat: a lesser known brand, and a driver is required.
products.skipIf: Brand support is important to you.

products.name: Anker Laptop Docking Station Dual Monitor, 8-in-1 USB C Hub
products.verdict: Dual HDMI, 85W Power Delivery and Gigabit Ethernet for little money.
products.description:
Anker's 8-in-1 has dual HDMI with 4K support, 85W Power Delivery, Gigabit Ethernet and an SD reader. The charger is not included.

It ranks seventh because on a base-chip Air a plain hub mirrors the second screen rather than extending it, so dual use is limited. It beats the UGREEN below on port count.

Best for a simple desk with one monitor and Ethernet. Caveat: confirm your Air supports two extended screens.
products.idealFor: One monitor, Ethernet and a card reader.
products.skipIf: You need two extended screens on a base chip.

products.name: UGREEN 10-in-1 USB C Docking Station, Revodok Pro 210
products.verdict: The smallest and cheapest pick here, with dual HDMI or one 8K output.
products.description:
The Revodok Pro 210 is a compact 10-in-1 hub with dual HDMI at 4K and 60Hz or a single 8K at 30Hz, 100W Power Delivery, 5Gbps data, Gigabit Ethernet and SD and TF readers.

It ranks last because it is a plain hub, and 5Gbps is the slowest data speed here. In its favor, it is the smallest and the cheapest.

Best for travel and a single extra monitor. Caveat: dual display depends on your chip.
cons: Dual screens depend on your chip

whatMatters.detail: Most MacBook Air chips drive one external display natively. A hub that advertises dual HDMI will usually mirror the second screen on those, or extend it only with DisplayLink software. Check your Air's tech specs page for the supported external displays before choosing a dock.

DisplayLink adds extra screens by compressing video through a driver. It works well for documents and video calls but can stutter on fast video and needs a one-time install. If you only need one screen, skip it and take a native dock.

A MacBook Air needs far less than a Pro, roughly 30 to 45W. Any dock giving 65W or more charges it with room to spare. Look for passthrough wattage in the specs, and for a bundled charger if you want to avoid carrying a second brick.
Some docks list support for M1 through M4 or M5 specifically. Check that your chip appears on the list, and that macOS is current, since driver support follows the OS.
5Gbps is fine for a keyboard and a mouse. If you copy photos or video to an SSD, look for 10Gbps ports or Thunderbolt. Compare the ports' stated speeds before buying.

faq.q: Can a MacBook Air run two external monitors?
faq.a: Natively, most cannot. With DisplayLink docks like the TobenONE 18-in-2 you can, at the cost of a driver and compression.

faq.q: Do I need a Thunderbolt dock for a MacBook Air?
faq.a: Not unless you want a fast single-screen dock. The Plugable TBT-UDM is the Thunderbolt option, and cheaper hubs cover the basics.

faq.q: Is the TobenONE worth more than the PULWTOP?
faq.a: If you want a charger included and faster Ethernet, yes. For just two screens, the PULWTOP is enough.

faq.q: Will a hub charge my Air while docked?
faq.a: Yes, through passthrough Power Delivery. An Air needs about 30 to 45W, which every dock here exceeds.

faq.q: Does DisplayLink work well for video?
faq.a: It handles documents and calls fine but can struggle with fast motion. Prefer native output for gaming or video editing.

faq.q: Can I use these docks with a Windows PC?
faq.a: The Anker DL6350 and WAVLINK both list Windows support. Check each listing before assuming.

finalTake: For most MacBook Air owners who need one monitor and fast connectivity, the Plugable TBT-UDM is the best buy: certified Thunderbolt 4, 100W charging and no drivers. If you need two screens, the TobenONE 18-in-2 is the strongest choice, and the Anker DL6350 stretches to three. On a budget, the PULWTOP is the cheapest dual-screen route.
